final_proof:
Let the mass distribution of the body be denoted by \(d\mu(x)\), so that \(\int_B d\mu=M\). Let \(C\) be its centre of mass. Thus, by the definition of centre of mass,
\[
\int_B (x-C)\,d\mu(x)=0.
\]
Choose a unit vector \(u\) in the common direction of the two parallel axes. Since \(A\) passes through \(C\), it has the form
\[
A=C+\mathbb R u.
\]
Because \(A'\) is parallel to \(A\), there is a unique vector \(a\) perpendicular to \(u\) such that
\[
A'=C+a+\mathbb R u.
\]
Indeed, \(C+a\) is the point obtained by moving perpendicularly from \(A\) to \(A'\). Consequently, \(|a|\) is the distance between the axes, so \(|a|=l\).

Let \(P\) denote orthogonal projection onto the plane perpendicular to \(u\):
\[
P(v)=v-(v\cdot u)u.
\]
For any point \(x\), its squared distance from a line having direction \(u\) is the squared norm of the projection, onto \(u^\perp\), of the displacement from any point on that line. Hence, writing \(r=x-C\),
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,A)^2=|P(r)|^2
\]
and, because \(P(a)=a\),
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,A')^2=|P(r-a)|^2=|P(r)-a|^2.
\]
Using the definition of moment of inertia and expanding the square therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
I
&=\int_B |P(x-C)-a|^2\,d\mu(x)\\
&=\int_B |P(x-C)|^2\,d\mu(x)
 -2a\cdot\int_B P(x-C)\,d\mu(x)
 +|a|^2\int_B d\mu(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
The first term is \(I_0\). Linearity of the projection and the centre-of-mass identity give
\[
\int_B P(x-C)\,d\mu(x)
=P\!\left(\int_B(x-C)\,d\mu(x)\right)
=P(0)=0.
\]
Finally, the last term is \(|a|^2M=l^2M\). Thus
\[
\boxed{I=I_0+Ml^2}.
\]
